songwriter: Traditional Sufi invocations and interpolated verses
original_format: Qawwali party (lead singer, chorus, harmonium, tabla)
research_notes: Several distinct qawwalis share this title. Nusrat's version was composed in the early 1970s and became a staple of his live repertoire; live recordings issued by Oriental Star Agencies after his 1985 UK tour, studio recording 1988 (per English Wikipedia). The refrain is a traditional Sufi dhikr, so authorship of the text is not solely Nusrat's. Year left empty because composition is given only as 'early 1970s'. Sabri Brothers recorded a different 'Allah Hoo' on the 1978 album Qawwali: Sufi Music from Pakistan.

research_notes: From the soundtrack of Dil Se.. (1998), directed by Mani Ratnam. Music A. R. Rahman, lyrics Gulzar after the Sufi poem/song 'Tere Ishq Nachaya' by Bulleh Shah. Sung by Sukhwinder Singh and Sapna Awasthi; recorded at Panchathan Record Inn. Year 1998 is the film/soundtrack release year. South Asian film song, so filed here rather than in film_tv_animation.csv.

subgenre: Kriti in raga Hamsadhvani, Adi tala
research_notes: Kriti by Muthuswami Dikshitar (one of the Carnatic Trinity) in Hamsadhvani, Adi tala, in praise of Vatapi Ganapati at Tiruvarur. Carnatica.net essay (2004) is the source consulted; exact composition year not given there, so year is empty. Common opening invocatory piece after the varnam in Carnatic concerts.

Title song of Raj Kapoor's film Awaara, sung by Mukesh. English Wikipedia credits lyrics to Shailendra and music to Shankar–Jaikishan, and the film page dates the picture to 14 December 1951 and lists the song in raga Bhairavi. The Hindi film-song database Hamraaz lists the same singer, lyricist and music directors for the 1951 film. South Asian film songs are kept in this regional file. Year is the film's release year.

Sufi song in honour of Lal Shahbaz Qalandar of Sehwan. English Wikipedia says no recording or document of the poem is known before the 1950s, while shrine legend attributes an original to Amir Khusrow and a later reshaping to Bulleh Shah. Urdu Wikipedia repeats that legend and says the tune now commonly heard is associated with Ustad Ashiq Hussain. No author or year is entered. Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan later recorded it; this row is the traditional song, not one of his albums. Harmonium and tabla are the usual qawwali pair and are not taken from a single session credit.

title_original: যদি তোর ডাক শুনে কেউ না আসে তবে একলা চলো রে
title_english: Jodi tor dak shune keu na ase (Ekla Cholo Re)
research_notes: Rabindra Sangeet written by Rabindranath Tagore in 1905 at Giridih, first published as Eka in the September 1905 Bhandar, later song 3 of the Swadesh section of Gitabitan. Tagoreweb gives raga Baul, tala dadra, Bengali year 1312, and notation by Indira Devi. Onushilon dates the writing to 26 Bhadra 1312 at Giridih, during the anti-partition movement. A cylinder by Tagore for H. Bose Swadeshi Records, made sometime between 1905 and 1908, is lost. The song is sung in Bangladesh as well as India. Year is the publication year.

Fifth of Tyagaraja's Pancharatna kritis. Telugu text, Sri raga, Adi tala. The pallavi salutes the many great souls. One account says he sang it at once in 1838 after hearing Shatkala Govinda Marar at Tiruvaiyaru. The Pancharatna page records a conflicting Walajapet account that disciples already knew the kriti before Marar arrived, and that it was an early work. Year is therefore empty. Concert accompaniments vary and are not listed.

Nepali folk song. English Wikipedia says Buddhi Pariyar composed it after collecting it around Pokhara, and that Sunder Shrestha and Dwarika Lal Joshi first performed it in 1969, with sarangi, madal and bansuri. A Nepali essay on Nepal Namcha says it is unclear whether Pariyar wrote the song or only collected it, that a firm first-recording date is not documented, and that one Radio Nepal account names Sunder Shrestha with Santosh Basnet rather than Joshi. Year 1969 follows the English Wikipedia release line and is flagged by that conflict. Not a Narayan Gopal song.

Playback song by Lata Mangeshkar for the 1964 Hindi film Woh Kaun Thi?, music Madan Mohan, lyrics Raja Mehdi Ali Khan, label Saregama. Picturised on Sadhana and Manoj Kumar. A line on the song page that the tune is in raga Pahari is marked citation needed and is not used. The YouTube upload of the film sequence repeats the same credits. Year is the film year given on the song page; a day was not stated.

National anthem of Bangladesh. Words by Rabindranath Tagore. Both language editions say the manuscript is lost, so the exact writing day is unknown, and that the melody comes from the Baul singer Gagan Harkara's Ami kothay pabo tare. Bengali Wikipedia, citing Prashanta Kumar Pal, says it was first sung on 25 August 1905 at a Kolkata Town Hall reading and printed in Sanjibani on 7 September 1905; it was in the 1905 book Baul. The first ten lines were chosen as the anthem on 13 January 1972 and adopted officially in 1972. Written at Shilaidaha in Nadia, now in Bangladesh. Year 1905 is the publication year, not a dated autograph. Second song in this file for Tagore.

Patriotic pop song by Vital Signs, sung by Junaid Jamshed. BBC Urdu and the Express Tribune place the PTV commission and the 14 August broadcast in 1987; Urdu Wikipedia says August 1987; Apple Music dates a release 14 August 1987. Lyrics by Nisar Nasik, with Shoaib Mansoor producing and reshaping the refrain. The Tribune says Nusrat Hussain wrote the tune that was kept, after a first tune was rejected. English Wikipedia's infobox says August 1985, which these other pages do not support, so 1987 is used and the status stays partial. Not the state anthem.

March song by Kazi Nazrul Islam, known by the opening চল্ চল্ চল্. Nazrul Kosh says he wrote it in the first week of February 1928 at Syed Abul Hosen's house in Dhaka, for the Muslim Sahitya Samaj conference; it first appeared in Shikha (Baishakh 1335 / April–May 1928) as Notuner Gaan and in the book Sandhya (August 1929). English Wikipedia dates words and tune to 1928. Dadra tala. Adopted as Bangladesh's national march on 13 January 1972. The lyric names a madol. The English page URL redirects from Chol Chol Chol to Notuner Gaan. Year is the 1928 writing, not the 1929 book.

title_english: Pyar kiya to darna kya (Why Fear When You Have Loved)
research_notes: Song from the film Mughal-e-Azam, sung by Lata Mangeshkar with a chorus, music Naushad, lyrics Shakeel Badayuni. The song page dates the release to 5 August 1960 and says it is picturised on Madhubala. The soundtrack page sets it in raga Durga and says Naushad reshaped a folk line from eastern Uttar Pradesh, Prem kiya, kya chori kari hai. Hindi Wikipedia lists the same singer, composer and duration of 6:21. Second song in this file for Lata Mangeshkar.

title_english: Euta mancheko mayale kati (How Much One Person's Love Changes a Life)
research_notes: Sung by Narayan Gopal. Annapurna Post reports composer Deepak Jangam's account that the lyric came from the palace, that he hid the writer's name while making tunes, and that the kept recording was एउटा मान्छेको मायाले कति फरक पर्दछ जिन्दगीमा, made at Music Nepal and paid for by the palace. A lyrics page names the writer as Chadani Shah, the pen name of Queen Aishwarya, and the same composer and label. No year is stated on either page. Nepali adhunik was added to the genre list. His English biography names the album Manche Ko Maya but not this title.

Song from the nurthi play Sirisangabo. Sinhala Wikipedia dates that play to 1903 and lists it among John de Silva's works; it does not print this lyric. Divaina quotes the opening දන්නෝ බුදුන්ගේ and says it is from Sirisangabo. A song blog gives the same lyric, credits the words to John de Silva and the tune to Vishwanath Lawjee, and names a later performance by W. D. Amaradeva. The tune credit and the Amaradeva performance rest on that blog, so the status stays partial. Sinhala nurthi was added to the genre list. Kept in the regional file as a Sinhala stage song.

title_english: Jat gelo jat gelo bole (Caste Is Gone, They Say)
research_notes: Baul song quoted on the Bengali biography of Lalon, opening জাত গেল জাত গেল বলে / একি আজব কারখানা, and ending লালন বলে জাত কারে কয়. The page gives his dates as 1774 to 17 October 1890 and places his akhra at Cheuriya in Kushtia, now Bangladesh. It does not date this song, so the year is empty and the decade is only the century of his life. No second page consulted here prints the same lyric.
